title: Thin-client structured calls and tool-snapshot playbook
content:
Purpose
This doc proposes a lightweight "thin-client" pattern for hosted streaming calls that expect structured tool outputs. The focus: a small, easy-to-adopt SDK surface for mobile/edge clients that provides resumable sessions via compact tool snapshots, explicit commit frames for structured outputs, and low-overhead telemetry suitable for constrained networks.

Problem statement
Teams building apps against the Hosted API have two recurring frictions:
- Mobile/edge clients suffer poor UX when incremental streaming interleaves tool calls and structured fragments: reconnects commonly produce duplicate tool invocations or lost partial results.
- Large SDKs or heavy session protocols increase binary size and cognitive load for app developers. There is demand for a minimal contract that still enables: resumability, idempotent tool semantics, typed structured outputs, and observability for debugging regressions.

Goals
- Define a compact wire/SDK contract for streaming sessions with structured outputs and tool calls that mobile/edge teams can implement with ~100–300 lines of code.
- Provide a snapshot mechanism for tool state (tool-snapshots) that lets clients resume without re-running full toolgraphs.
- Make tool invocations idempotent by explicit action ids and commit/rollback frames.
- Instrument low-cost telemetry hooks (event counters and sampled spans) for developer debugging without blowing bandwidth.

Non-goals
- Full-featured distributed transactions or multi-client real-time collaboration.
- Complex client-side orchestration libraries — this is intentionally small and opinionated.

High-level design
1) Small frame types (streaming frames over WS or HTTP/2 stream):
   - CONTROL: handshake, keepalive, resume-request, resume-ack
   - DELTA: incremental text/markdown fragments (best-effort)
   - STRUCT: structured payload (json-schema-constrained) with fragment_id and optional parent_id
   - TOOL_CALL: tool invocation request (tool_id, action_id, args_snapshot_id)
   - TOOL_SNAPSHOT: compact representation of tool-local results or provenance (snapshot_id, compressed-json-base64)
   - COMMIT: commits a particular STRUCT or TOOL_CALL result (id, signature)
   - ROLLBACK: explicit rollback hint for a previously committed id (rare but useful for tool fallback)
   - CHECKPOINT: periodic small checkpoints for resume validation (checkpoint_id, last_applied_id)

2) Action ids & snapshots
   - Every tool_call must include a stable action_id generated client-side (UUIDv4 or deterministic hash). Server echoes action_id in TOOL_CALL responses. This lets clients deduplicate on resume.
   - TOOL_SNAPSHOT is an opaque but versioned blob created by the host when a tool produces an intermediate representation (e.g., parsed search results, database rows, structured annotations). Snapshots can be referenced by args_snapshot_id in subsequent tool_calls to avoid re-sending large contexts.

3) Commit semantics (idempotent + observable)
   - For structured outputs (STRUCT), the runtime requires an explicit COMMIT to make that STRUCT visible to downstream consumers (billing/analytics and SDK state).
   - COMMIT includes a compact signature (hash of payload + action_id) allowing servers and clients to assert consistency on resume.
   - Until COMMIT is seen, STRUCT frames are considered provisional and may be replayed after resume.

4) Resume flow (thin-client friendly)
   - Client reconnects with resume-request including last_checkpoint_id and last_committed_id.
   - Server replies with resume-ack and an ordered list of missing COMMITs and recent TOOL_SNAPSHOT ids (if any) the client can request.
   - Client replays only missing action_ids for TOOL_CALL. If a matching COMMIT is present server-side, server returns the committed STRUCT/TOOL_SNAPSHOT rather than re-executing.

5) Prefetch & speculative behavior
   - Clients may request speculative prefetch of expected tool_snapshots by providing a small hint (prefetch_hint string) in handshake. Server returns small indexes or metadata about cached snapshots to avoid full re-execution.

6) Telemetry (minimal by default)
   - Counters: requests_sent, tool_calls_inflight, commits_applied, resume_attempts
   - Sampled traces: 1% by default for sessions that include tool calls; include action_id and checkpoint_id in trace context.
   - SDK exposes a single callback to report these counters periodically; server-side supports sampled debug dumps keyed by action_id.

API surface (SDK ergonomics)
- Minimal JS/Swift/Kotlin API shape (pseudo):
  - connect(session_params, handlers) -> connection
  - handlers.onDelta(fragment) -> apply to local UI
  - handlers.onStruct(structPayload, meta) -> buffer until commit
  - handlers.onToolCall(toolCall) -> optional local handler or forward to server
  - connection.commit(structId) -> sends COMMIT frame
  - connection.toolSnapshotRequest(snapshotId) -> fetch snapshot blob
  - connection.resume(last_checkpoint_id, last_committed_id) -> resume flow

Design choices for ergonomics
- Default to optimistic UI: STRUCTs are surfaced immediately but marked "provisional" until commit returns; minimal local state: store last committed id and last checkpoint id.
- Keep binary footprint small: core types + tiny serializer for frame types (length-prefixed msgpack/CBOR recommended). SDK helper only implements framing + idempotency checks; apps manage UI state.
- Backpressure: provide max_inflight limit and simple queueing. On constrained networks, SDK drops DELTA frames older than last committed id (best-effort).

Failure modes and mitigation
- Duplicate tool execution on resume: if client re-sends a tool_call with same action_id, server must check existing committed snapshot or result and return it if present.
- Missing snapshots: TOOL_SNAPSHOT blobs are garbage-collected after TTL; server may return a snapshot-missing error pointing to fallback (re-run tool or accept degraded output). SDK surfaces clear diagnostics.
- Network partitions: periodic CHECKPOINT frames permit fast resume windows; shorter checkpoint intervals improve UX at cost of bandwidth.

Migration guidance for host teams
- New hosted endpoints should accept both legacy streaming and the thin-client frames. Use content negotiation (Accept: application/redwood-thin+json) to enable the protocol per-client.
- Provide a compatibility fallback: if client doesn't pass action_id, server should fall back to stateless streaming but emit a deprecation warning in telemetry.

Rollout plan (3 sprints)
- Sprint 1: implement wire framing and COMMIT semantics in backend + basic JS SDK prototype. Instrument counters.
- Sprint 2: server-side snapshot store + resume path and idempotency checks. Add sample Swift/Kotlin SDK shims.
- Sprint 3: field trials with two mid-size customers (mobile messaging client and note-taking app). Collect UX metrics (resume success rate, duplicate tool_call rate) and iterate.

Open questions
- Snapshot size limits and compression: do we enforce a hard max (e.g., 64KB) for TOOL_SNAPSHOT to keep network predictable?
- Security: should snapshots be encrypted per-tenant (affects replayability across Dedicated/Private)?
- Billing implications: are provisional STRUCT frames chargeable before COMMIT? (recommendation: charge on COMMIT only).

Appendix: sample handshake (pseudo-JSON)
Client -> Server: CONTROL(handshake): {client: "tiny-sdk/0.1", accept: "redwood-thin/1", last_checkpoint: "cp-42", resume_hint: "session-123"} 
Server -> Client: CONTROL(resume-ack): {accepted: true, missing_commits: ["c-63"], available_snapshots: ["s-12"]} 
TOOL_CALL example: {type: "TOOL_CALL", tool_id: "search-v1", action_id: "a-9f7", args_snapshot_id: "s-12"} 
COMMIT example: {type: "COMMIT", id: "c-63", signature: "sha256:...", related_action: "a-9f7"} 

Notes and next steps
- Aim to keep the initial SDK implementation < 10 KB minified for JS and a couple KB for mobile languages.
- Prepare a developer guide with a small reference implementation that demonstrates: unstable network resume, idempotent tool calls, and commit/rollback flows.
- Schedule a cross-team review with serving-runtime and privacy/security to resolve snapshot encryption and retention policy.

Author notes (brainstorm):
This playbook tries to balance production needs (idempotency, observability) with the constraints of thin clients. It intentionally shifts some complexity back to the app: SDK remains small and opinionated, but apps must store last-committed ids and checkpoint ids. The goal is practical: fewer duplicated tool runs, clearer diagnostics, and a straightforward migration path from existing streaming patterns.
